catalog_quote: Chamorro is a language with stress. Each word has one syllable that bears primary stress (i.e. is louder or more prominent than the other syllables in the word). This syllable is generally the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of the word. Primary stress is determined differently for roots (unaffixed words) than for affixed words. A substantial number of roots, most of them borrowed from Spanish, exceptionally have primary stress on the last syllable. ... /aˈsut/ ... A substantial number of roots exceptionally have primary stress on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable. ... /ˈdeddigu/ ... /aˈpigigiʔ/ ... /ˈkunanaf/ ... All other roots have primary stress on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable. ... /ˈsajna/ ... /iˈlotis/ ... /kaˈdidak/ ... In affixed words, primary stress is determined by whether the affix is a suffix, an inherently stressed prefix, or some other morpheme…
sweep_summary: Two title hits, both by known Chamorro specialists. (1) Chung 2003 (LI 34) was fetched sources from the author's UCSC page (Semantic Scholar green-OA link; saved with text layer). It is a syntax/prosody paper on weak-pronoun clitics; its single word-stress statement (p. 579-580: primary stress 'calculated from the right', falling on the penult of the prosodic word) confirms the catalog's penultimate coding but supplies nothing on exceptions. (2) Crosswhite 1998 (Phonology 15) is paywalled at Cambridge (Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar closed, no ROA copy); the abstract says it analyzes Saipanese Chamorro stress shifts under affixation in correspondence theory - a theoretical treatment that would refine the affixation facts but is unlikely to beat Chung 2020 as the deciding statement (priority medium). Note on the deciding source itself: re-reading Chung 2020 sec. 29.4.1 (pp. 660-663; excerpt saved) shows the catalog quote is truncated after the final-stress loans; the section continues 'A substantial number of roots exceptionally have primary stress on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable' (e.g. /ˈdeddigu/, /ˈkunanaf/), stressed prefixes (a-, acha-, mi-, sen, gof, gai, tai...) take primary stress, and suffixes re-place stress on the penult of the suffixed word - i.e. the deciding source states substantial lexical exceptions in both directions, which the 'fixed-strict' register (exceptions falsify) should weigh; the record already carries lexical_stress='disputed'. lookups used Crossref, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Cambridge Core, ROA index and direct fetches.

A one-line confirmation by the same author as the catalog's deciding source, embedded in a paper about clitic placement; it gives no account of exceptions, so it adds nothing beyond Chung 2020 sec. 29.4.1.

sources.citation: Chung, Sandra. 2003. The Syntax and Prosody of Weak Pronouns in Chamorro. Linguistic Inquiry 34(4): 547-599.
sources.quote: Prosodic words in Chamorro are distinguished by the fact that they bear primary stress, which is calculated from the right. Among the many Chamorro processes sensitive to primary stress is the reduplication that realizes progressive aspect. When a predicate XP in Chamorro is inflected for progressive aspect, the inflection is realized on the leftmost prosodic word instantiating the XP, via reduplication of its primarily stressed CV (i.e., the onset and nucleus of the primarily stressed syllable, but not the coda). [p. 580:] (Had the combination of adjective and noun formed a single prosodic word, that word's primary stress would have fallen on the initial syllable of patgun 'child'; compare (58a).)
sources.locator: p. 579 (section 6.1, paragraph before ex. (57)); p. 580 (parenthetical after ex. (59))
sources.note: The paper is about the syntax and prosodic phrasing of weak (clitic) pronouns, not a description of word stress. Its only word-stress statement is that each prosodic word bears one primary stress 'calculated from the right'; the p. 580 example (stress would fall on the initial = penultimate syllable of a hypothetical adjective+noun prosodic word, patgun being disyllabic) shows the right-edge computation is penultimate. Weak pronouns are 'prosodically deficient enclitics: unstressed forms, mostly monosyllables' (p. 548). No exceptions or lexical-stress discussion.

sources.note: Per the Cambridge abstract page: a correspondence-theoretic (OT) paper on the Saipanese dialect of Chamorro, examining cases where the location of stress shifts under affixation, so that 'the linear order of segments would remain the same in both words, but the location of the prosodic heads would differ'; argues Chamorro phonology needs both segmental and prosodic correspondence. The abstract does not state where primary stress falls; the body presumably builds on the Chung 1983 / Topping 1973 description (penultimate default, lexical exceptions, stress shift under suffixation).
